content: The financial costs associated with the introduction and deployment of IPTsc include expenses related to engaging communities, parents, and school teachers. The cost-effectiveness of combining IPTsc with other school health programs should be evaluated. Alternative strategies for delivering malaria chemoprevention to school-aged children need to be assessed for both cost and feasibility. The development of drugs suitable for chemoprevention in school-aged children is essential. The impact of IPTsc on community-level malaria transmission should be studied. The effects of IPTsc on cognition and school performance in children require investigation. There is a need to develop malaria chemoprevention drugs that can be administered as a single dose. Approaches to safely include girls of reproductive age in IPTsc programs, including alternative regimens safe during pregnancy, should be explored. Post-discharge malaria chemoprevention (PDMC) involves administering a full antimalarial treatment course at regular intervals to children admitted with severe anemia. The goal of PDMC is to prevent new malaria infections in these children during the high-risk period following hospital discharge, reducing the likelihood of re-admission or death. Severe anemia, as defined by WHO, has a multifactorial etiology, and identifying the primary cause often requires further laboratory tests, including a complete blood cell count. PDMC should be administered even when the cause of severe anemia cannot be identified. Antimalarial medicines used for PDMC can be the same as first-line malaria treatments, but alternative medicines are preferred. SP, AL, and DHA-P were used in trials and found effective for PDMC. Local data on the age distribution of severe anemia should guide the target age group for PDMC. Dosage should be based on the child’s weight whenever possible, with age-based dosing used only when weight cannot be determined. Children on PDMC should receive a complete course of antimalarials at the recommended treatment dose. Children admitted to hospitals with severe anemia in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission can be given a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medicine at predetermined times post-discharge to reduce re-admission and mortality. PDMC should not be given to children whose severe anemia is due to blood loss from trauma, surgery, malignancy, or bleeding disorders. Implementation should consider the duration of protection provided by the selected antimalarial, as well as the feasibility and affordability of delivering additional PDMC courses. Moderate to high malaria transmission settings are defined as areas with a Plasmodium falciparum parasite prevalence greater than 10% or an annual parasite incidence exceeding 250 per 1,000. These thresholds are indicative and not absolute for determining PDMC applicability. The frequency of PDMC administration should be informed by the protective efficacy of the selected drug, the transmission season duration, and the feasibility of delivering additional treatments. Trials have evaluated different PDMC regimens, including SP administered monthly starting seven days post-discharge, AL given at discharge and at four and eight weeks post-discharge, and a combination of AL at discharge followed by DHA-P monthly starting 14 days post-discharge. Two delivery approaches for PDMC have been evaluated: community-based and facility-based. In community-based delivery, caregivers receive all PDMC courses at discharge with instructions and administration dates written on the child’s health card. In facility-based delivery, caregivers must collect PDMC drugs from a health facility each month. Community-based delivery was found to be more cost-saving due to reduced travel costs and higher adherence rates. However, caregiver literacy may pose challenges for equitable delivery, as some caregivers may struggle to read administration dates on health cards. SMS reminders may also raise equity concerns. The impact of drug resistance on PDMC’s protective efficacy is unclear. However, the selective pressure exerted by PDMC on the parasite population is likely small due to the relatively limited population eligible for PDMC compared to other malaria chemoprevention interventions. Children with sickle cell disease should be included in PDMC unless they are already receiving regular chemoprevention for their condition. PDMC is not recommended for children who develop severe acute illness post-discharge, cannot take oral medication, have received a dose of the PDMC drug in the last 30 days, or are allergic to the PDMC drugs. PDMC-SP should not be given to individuals on sulfa-based medications, such as co-trimoxazole for HIV. Information about PDMC should be fully accessible to caregivers, and consent should be obtained before administration. Evidence from trials indicates that PDMC reduces re-admissions and mortality during the intervention period. Caregivers generally have positive views of PDMC, understanding its value in preventing malaria during the post-discharge period. Community health workers (CHWs) also view PDMC as beneficial, though adherence to home visit reminders is often poor due to barriers such as inadequate training, lack of supervision, and high workloads. Community-based PDMC delivery is potentially more equitable than facility-based delivery, as it reduces the burden of repeated travel to health facilities. However, PDMC may reinforce existing health inequities, as it is administered to children who have already accessed hospital care. Among those with hospital access, the intervention is likely equitable. Community-based delivery resulted in higher adherence rates compared to facility-based delivery, though potential stigma from repeated CHW visits may be a concern. The WHO guidelines for malaria, developed using the GRADE framework, recommend PDMC based on evidence from systematic reviews and contextual factors. The intervention is considered cost-effective, though the certainty of evidence regarding resource requirements is low. Further information on PDMC implementation, equity, and cost-effectiveness can be found in associated unpublished evidence and reports.
